screens.title: Essential CLI Navigation and File Management
screens.narratorSegment: The command line is the primary tool you'll use as an RHCSA. In this chapter we focus on navigating the Linux filesystem and managing files safely. You will learn how to find where you are, move around using absolute and relative paths, list directory contents with detailed options, create and remove files and folders, and inspect file contents without overwhelming the terminal. We emphasize safe patterns for deletion and common pitfalls that new administrators encounter. For example, you will see how the print working directory command tells you the exact path you occupy, how the change directory command accepts both absolute paths from the root and relative paths from your current folder, and why pagers like less are preferable for huge logs. Practice sequences from creating nested directories to moving a file and viewing it are included so you can build muscle memory. By the end of this chapter you will have a small set of commands that let you explore, inspect, modify, and clean up a RHEL system with confidence and care.

Practice and Safety Objectives

Create

screens.title: The Linux filesystem tree and root directory
screens.narratorSegment: The Linux filesystem is a single tree that starts at the root directory, known as forward slash. Everything on the system — configuration files, user data, binaries, devices — branches from that root. Understanding this single-root model helps you reason about absolute and relative paths. An absolute path starts at the root and lists every directory to the target, for example forward slash etc forward slash hosts. A relative path describes how to reach the target from where you currently are, using names and the special entries dot and dot dot to mean the current and parent directory. Practically, this matters because commands like change directory and file operations can accept either form. When you use absolute paths you remove ambiguity — you always operate on the same location regardless of where you are. Relative paths are faster to type and often more convenient during interactive work, but they depend on your current working directory. A common misconception is that home is the root; it is not. Home is just a directory under root, typically under slash home slash yourusername. Learning to read and compose both absolute and relative paths avoids mistakes when moving or deleting files and helps you write reliable scripts. Think about building a mental map: when you see a path, imagine the branch sequence from the root to the leaf and verify before you act.

keyIdea.text: Root (/) is the single origin; absolute paths are unambiguous, relative paths are contextual and faster interactively.

content.html:
Core Concept

Filesystem tree and root directory

Treat the filesystem as a single rooted tree starting at '/'. This mental model clarifies absolute vs relative paths.

Key definitions
  • Root (/): the top-most directory containing all files and directories.
  • Absolute path: begins with '/', lists each directory from root to target.
  • Relative path: listed from current working directory; uses '.' and '..' for current and parent.
Example: Absolute path: /etc/hosts — the hosts file in system config.
Example: Relative path: ../config refers to a sibling directory of the current folder.
Annotated path cards
Absolute
/etc/sysconfig/network-scripts
Use when you must be unambiguous about location.
Relative
../config or my_project/data
Use for quick local navigation, but verify pwd when uncertain.
Key Takeaway

Always confirm your current working directory before running destructive commands that use relative paths.

Common misconception

Home is not root. Home is ~/. It is often /home/youruser, which is a branch under root. Using absolute paths prevents confusion about where operations will run.

screens.title: Using pwd and cd to control your context
screens.narratorSegment: Knowing your current directory and being able to change it reliably is a daily task. The print working directory command reports the absolute path to your shell's current location; use it to confirm context before running scripts or editing files. The change directory command accepts an absolute path or a relative one. For example, cd /etc moves to the system configuration folder, while cd projects moves to a child directory in your current folder. Special shortcuts speed up navigation: cd tilde returns you to your home directory regardless of where you are. cd double dot moves you up one level, useful for stepping out of nested folders quickly. cd hyphen toggles back to the previous directory you were in — that is handy during troubleshooting when you hop between two locations. When you chain these commands in a session, a reliable pattern is to run pwd, then cd to the target, then run pwd again to verify. A common error is assuming cd without arguments always does nothing; it actually moves you to your home directory. Another pitfall is forgetting how relative paths change meaning based on your current directory. Practice sequences such as creating a nested tree, moving into it, printing the working directory, and then returning using cd - will build this mental model. Ask yourself: before running a command that alters files, what path does pwd show and is that the intended location?

keyIdea.title: Context control
keyIdea.text: Use pwd to confirm and cd with absolute or relative paths to change context; use shortcuts (~, .., -) for speed and accuracy.

content.html:
Process Flow

pwd and cd — verify then move

A safe workflow: print your path, change directory, then confirm the new path.

Step-by-step
  1. Run pwd to see the current absolute path.
  2. Run cd with an absolute or relative path to move.
  3. Run pwd again to confirm you are in the expected directory.
  4. Use cd - to return to the previous directory when needed.
Example sequence
pwd
cd projects/web/html
pwd
cd -
Shortcuts and notes
  • cd ~ returns to your home directory.
  • cd .. moves up one level; repeat for higher levels.
  • cd - toggles to previous working directory.
Common mistake

Relying on relative paths without checking pwd can cause operations to run on the wrong files or directories.

Check your understanding

If you are in /home/cohortiauser/projects and type cd ../.. what is your new path? Answer by thinking of the tree structure and parent levels.

screens.title: Listing files: ls, hidden files, and long listings
screens.narratorSegment: Listing directory contents is more than seeing filenames. The basic list command shows names, but combining options reveals crucial metadata. Use ls -l to get a long listing that includes file permissions, number of links, owner, group, size, and modification time. This output helps you identify whether a file is writable, executable, or owned by another user. Hidden files, those that begin with a dot, are not shown by default; ls -a reveals them. Often you want both metadata and hidden entries, so ls -la or ls -al is the common combination. A frequent misunderstanding is mixing up the columns in ls -l: the first column shows permission bits and file type, not just an attribute label. The long listing prefix begins with a character denoting file type, like dash for a regular file or d for a directory, followed by permission triplets. Reading this line quickly is a necessary skill for troubleshooting permissions and diagnosing why a service can't read its configuration. Practice reading ls -l output and spotting whether a file is owned by root or your user, whether it is executable, and when it was last modified. If you cannot find a configuration file, remember to run ls -a to show dotfiles and avoid the common mistake of assuming the file does not exist.

keyIdea.title: List with context
keyIdea.text: Use ls -l and ls -a to reveal metadata and hidden files; interpret the permission string to diagnose access issues.

content.html:
Comparison

ls vs ls -l vs ls -a

Compare simple listing, long listing for metadata, and showing hidden files.

Example outputs
$ ls
bin  config  index.html

$ ls -l
-rw-r--r-- 1 cohortiauser cohortia  128 Jun  1 12:00 index.html
drwxr-xr-x 2 cohortiauser cohortia 4096 Jun  1 11:58 config

$ ls -la
drwxr-xr-x 3 cohortiauser cohortia 4096 Jun  1 11:58 .
-rw-r--r-- 1 cohortiauser cohortia  256 Jun  1 11:57 .bashrc
Key Takeaway

When troubleshooting permissions or missing files, combine ls -l and ls -a to reveal ownership and hidden entries.

How to read the first column in ls -l
  • First char: file type (d for directory, - for file).
  • Next nine chars: permission bits in three triplets for owner, group, others.
  • Use this to spot missing execute bits or other permission problems.
Common mistake

Not using -a when searching for config files leads to thinking files are missing. Hidden dotfiles often store user-level configurations.

Try this

Run ls -la in your home directory and identify any .bashrc or .profile files. Check ownership and modification time with ls -l.

screens.title: Creating directories and files: mkdir, rmdir, touch
screens.narratorSegment: Creating directories and empty files is routine. The make directory command creates directories by name. When you need to create nested parents in one step, use the -p option: mkdir -p /tmp/new_app/config will build any missing directories in the chain. Removing directories uses rmdir, but rmdir only succeeds when the target is empty. That behavior prevents accidental removal of nested content. When you want to delete non-empty directories, rm -r will remove recursively. Use rm -ri during practice to confirm each deletion, and never run rm -rf unless you are absolutely certain. To create an empty file or update its modification timestamp use touch filename. Touch is frequently used to create placeholder files like index. html before writing content. A practical sequence is to create a projects tree, cd into it, create nested web html css directories with mkdir -p, create three files with touch, then list contents with ls -la to confirm. A common misconception is that rmdir and rm are interchangeable; rmdir is safe for empty directories only and fails otherwise. Another pitfall is assuming mkdir will prompt before overwriting — it will not overwrite existing directories and will return success if the directory already exists unless prevented. Practice with small test directories and use interactive deletion to build safe habits.

keyIdea.title: Build and clean
keyIdea.text: Use mkdir -p for nested creation, touch for placeholders, and prefer interactive deletion to avoid data loss.

content.html:
Process Flow

mkdir, rmdir, touch — create and remove safely

A reliable flow: create nested folders, add placeholder files, verify contents, then remove using interactive deletion when testing.

Command examples
mkdir -p projects/web/html/css
cd projects/web/html
touch index.html style.css script.js
ls -la
rmdir empty_folder   # succeeds only if empty
rm -ri projects      # interactive recursive deletion
Key Takeaway

Prefer mkdir -p for nested creation and rm -ri for safe cleanup during learning.

When rmdir fails

rmdir will fail on non-empty directories. Use ls to inspect contents, then decide whether to remove individual files or use rm -r when appropriate.

Common mistake

Using rm -rf without checking the path can delete important data. Always confirm pwd and the target path before running destructive commands.

Try this

Create a small test tree with mkdir -p, add files with touch, then practice removing with rm -ri to observe prompts and confirm behaviors.

screens.title: Copying and moving files: cp and mv
screens.narratorSegment: Copy and move are often confused because they both change where data appears. The copy command duplicates files or directories, leaving the original in place. For a single file, cp source. txt destination. txt creates a new file with the same contents. When the destination is a directory, cp places the file inside it. Copying directories requires the recursive option: cp -r directory1 directory2 will duplicate the full tree. The move command renames or relocates files; mv oldname. txt newname. txt is a rename, while mv myfile. txt /tmp moves the file into another directory without keeping a second copy. Use cp when you need a backup or template, and mv when you want to change location or name without leaving a copy. A practical example: create index. html, then cp index. html about. html to make a second page for edits. After validating the copy, mv about. html public/about. html moves it into a deploy folder. A common misconception is believing cp automatically preserves metadata like ownership and timestamps; by default it copies content but options exist to preserve metadata if required. When copying system templates or skeletons, use cp -r to include nested content. Always confirm with ls -l that the expected files exist in the target and check sizes before assuming a successful copy. Practicing these sequences builds confidence that you are duplicating or relocating content deliberately, not accidentally losing the original.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

cp and mv — copy then move

Use copying for backups and templates, moving to relocate or rename without duplication.

Commands to try
touch index.html
cp index.html about.html    # create a duplicate
cp -r /etc/skel /home/newuser/profile_template    # recursive copy
mv about.html public/about.html    # move file into directory
ls -l public
Key Takeaway

Choose cp when you need a copy; choose mv to rename or relocate without keeping the original file in place.

Common pitfalls
  • Forgetting -r when copying directories results in an error or an incomplete operation.
  • Assuming cp preserves all metadata; use flags if ownership and timestamps must be retained.
Scenario

You have index.html and want a second page. Copy it to about.html, edit about.html, then move it into the public directory for deployment.

screens.title: Deleting files and directories safely with rm and rmdir
screens.narratorSegment: Deletion on the command line is powerful and potentially destructive. The remove command deletes files and, with -r, removes directories and their contents recursively. The -f option forces removal without prompting, which in combination with -r can irreversibly delete large directory trees. That is why cautious practices matter: use rm -ri while learning to prompt before each file is removed, and always check your current working directory with pwd before issuing a deletion command. rmdir exists to safely remove empty directories — it refuses to delete a directory that contains files, protecting you from accidental loss. A common dangerous habit is running rm -rf with an incorrectly typed path; for example, an accidental extra slash or missing variable expansion can delete unintended locations. A safer pattern is to list the target first with ls -la to confirm contents, then run rm with interactive mode or move the target to a temporary holding area before permanent removal. Remember, there is no easy undo for rm on most Linux systems without backups. Practice on disposable test trees and adopt the habit of interactive deletions until you are fully comfortable. The ultimate goal is to make deletions deliberate: inspect, confirm, then remove.

keyIdea.title: Safe deletion
keyIdea.text: Prefer rm -ri during practice and rmdir for empty directories; reserve rm -rf for controlled situations with backups.

content.html:
Core Concept

rm and rmdir — deletion with care

Deletion is permanent on most systems; confirm targets and use interactive modes during learning.

Examples and patterns
# Remove empty directory
rmdir temp_dir

# Interactive recursive deletion during practice
rm -ri projects

# Dangerous: force recursive deletion (use with extreme caution)
rm -rf important_data
Common mistake

Using rm -rf without verifying the path can remove system files or your home directory. Always pause and inspect what you're about to delete.

Pro tip

List the target with ls -la before deletion. Consider moving to a temporary archive folder first, then delete after verifying backups.

Key Takeaway

Deletion is permanent; make it deliberate by inspecting, prompting, and backing up when necessary.

screens.title: Viewing file contents: cat, less, and more
screens.narratorSegment: Inspecting file content is one of the most common tasks for administrators. The concatenate command displays a file's entire contents to standard output and is great for small files like configuration snippets. For large files, cat will dump everything and quickly flood your terminal, making it hard to find the lines you need. That's where pagers come in: less lets you scroll forward and backward, search for text with the slash command, and quit with q. More provides basic paging but lacks less's advanced navigation and search. Use less for large logs and files you want to explore interactively. A typical workflow is to view a log with less and search for an error keyword using slash error to jump to matches. You can also pipe output into less for paged viewing of command results. A misconception is thinking less opens files in edit mode — it is read-only by default. If you need to view a short file, cat file will work quickly; for any file that exceeds a terminal page, use less file. Practice example: cat /etc/os-release to view release metadata, and less /var/log/messages to page and search. Remember to quit less with q when you are finished. These habits help you inspect system state without losing your place or accidentally scrolldumping important context.

More provides basic paging but lacks less's advanced navigation and search. Use less for large logs and files you want to explore interactively. A typical workflow is to view a log with less and search for an error keyword using slash error to jump to matches. You can also pipe output into less for paged viewing of command results. A misconception is thinking less opens files in edit mode — it is read-only by default. If you need to view a short file, cat file will work quickly; for any file that exceeds a terminal page, use less file. Practice example: cat /etc/os-release to view release metadata, and less /var/log/messages to page and search. Remember to quit less with q when you are finished. These habits help you inspect system state without losing your place or accidentally scrolldumping important context.

Code Walkthrough

cat, less, more — pick the right viewer

Small file? Use cat. Large file or log? Use less for paging and searching.

Commands and tips
# View small files
cat /etc/os-release

# Page a large log
less /var/log/messages    # use /error to search, q to quit

# Pipe command output into less
dmesg | less
Key Takeaway

Prefer less for large files; learn basic navigation and search keys to find content quickly.

Example scenario

Troubleshooting a service: open /var/log/messages with less, search for the service name, and note timestamps around failures to correlate events.

Common misconception

less does not edit files. It is a pager for safe, read-only exploration. Use an editor to make changes after confirming the file and its location.

screens.title: Identifying file types with file and using ls -l for attributes
screens.narratorSegment: Before opening or executing a file, it's useful to know what type it is. The file command inspects the content and reports a human-readable type, such as ASCII text or ELF 64-bit executable. This quick check helps you avoid attempting to open a binary with a text editor or accidentally executing the wrong file. Use file /bin/bash to confirm a binary and file /etc/passwd to confirm text format. For ownership and access control information, ls -l provides the permission bits and owner and group information. Read the permission triplets to know whether the owner, the group, and others have read, write, or execute access. For example, a leading dash followed by rw- r-- r-- indicates an ordinary file with read/write for owner and read-only for group and others. These two commands together give you both the content classification and the access context. A common misconception is that file extension determines type on Linux; Linux relies on content and metadata not extensions. When preparing to run a script, verify it is a text script and that it has the execute bit set for the intended user. This practice reduces trial-and-error and avoids permission errors or accidental binary edits.

content.html:
Definition

file and ls -l — content and context

Use file to learn what a file contains; use ls -l to learn who can access it and when it changed.

Examples
$ file /bin/bash
/bin/bash: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64

$ file /etc/passwd
/etc/passwd: ASCII text

$ ls -l /etc/passwd
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 2768 Jun 1 10:00 /etc/passwd
Common misconception

File extensions are not authoritative on Linux. Rely on file and permissions to decide how to open or execute a file.

Practical check

Before executing a script, run file scriptname and then ls -l to confirm it is text and has an execute bit for your user.

Key Takeaway

Inspect both type and permissions — one tells you what it is, the other who can do what with it.

screens.title: Hands-on practice: build, move, view, and clean up
screens.narratorSegment: Practice sequencing builds habits. Follow a small, safe workflow on your lab VM: start in your home directory, confirm with pwd, and list contents with ls -la. Create a projects folder with mkdir -p projects/web/html/css and navigate into it. Create three placeholder files with touch index. html style. css script. js. Use echo to write a short string into index. html and then cat it to verify the content. Duplicate index. html as about. html using cp index. html about. html, then rename script. js to app. js with mv. Use ls -l to inspect ownership and sizes. Next, view a system file like /etc/hosts with cat or use less on a larger file to practice paging and searching. Finally, clean up the test tree with rm -ri projects, confirm prompts, and verify removal with ls. Each step reinforces a command, expects a predictable result, and includes a verification step before moving on. A common error is omitting verification; always check with ls, cat, or file to ensure the command behaved as expected. This structured practice will make the commands feel natural and reduce the chance of mistakes on real systems.

keyIdea.title: Practice sequence
keyIdea.text: Build a small tree, create files, copy, move, inspect contents, then remove with interactive deletion to validate each step.

content.html:
Process Flow

Hands-on practice sequence

A safe sequence to run on your lab VM that includes verification after each step.

Step list
  1. pwd and ls -la to confirm starting point.
  2. mkdir -p projects/web/html/css and cd into projects/web/html.
  3. touch index.html style.css script.js and echo "Hello RHEL!" > index.html.
  4. cat index.html to verify content.
  5. cp index.html about.html and mv script.js app.js.
  6. ls -l to confirm files and sizes.
  7. View /etc/hosts with cat and a large log with less to practice paging.
  8. Cleanup: cd ~ then rm -ri projects and verify removal with ls.
Example command block
pwd
mkdir -p projects/web/html/css
cd projects/web/html
touch index.html style.css script.js
echo "Hello RHEL!" > index.html
cat index.html
cp index.html about.html
mv script.js app.js
ls -l
cd ~
rm -ri projects
Safety reminder

Practice on non-critical files and use interactive deletion until you are comfortable with recursive removal.

screens.title: Assessment scenario and command sequence practice
screens.narratorSegment: Assessment practice helps you demonstrate competency. The scenario: you are in your home directory and must create a nested directory reports/2023/q4, move summary. txt into q4, change into that directory, and display its contents. The correct command sequence is mkdir -p reports/2023/q4 then mv summary. txt reports/2023/q4/ then cd reports/2023/q4 and finally cat summary. txt to view it. Each command has a specific role: mkdir -p constructs parents without error, mv relocates the file, cd establishes context for follow-on commands, and cat displays the file so you can confirm success. When grading, check that learners used mkdir -p instead of multiple mkdir calls, and that they verified the final location with pwd or ls before using cat. A second assessment asks how to inspect a large log without loading it entirely; the answer is less /var/log/syslog and then using the slash search to find error occurrences. For both tasks insist on the verification step: listing or printing the working directory before and after moves prevents accidental mistakes. Use these assessments to confirm that command sequences are correct, safe, and include verification.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Remember three core ideas: first, the filesystem is a single rooted tree beginning at root. Use absolute paths when you need certainty and relative paths for speed, but always verify with pwd. Second, choose the right file operation: use mkdir -p to create nested directories, cp -r to duplicate trees, mv to rename or relocate without copying, and rm with interactive flags during practice to avoid irreversible deletions. Third, inspect before acting: ls -l and file reveal permissions, ownership, and type; cat and less let you view content safely. Practicing short sequences that include verification after each command will make these patterns second nature and reduce costly mistakes on production systems. Ask yourself after each change: did I check where I was, what I changed, and can I recover if necessary? That habit separates careful administrators from careless ones.

What to Remember

Confirm Context

The command line is the primary tool you'll use as an RHCSA. In this chapter we focus on navigating the Linux filesystem and managing files safely. You will learn how to find where you are, move around using absolute and relative paths, list directory contents with detailed options, create and remove files and folders, and inspect file contents without overwhelming the terminal. We emphasize safe patterns for deletion and common pitfalls that new administrators encounter. For example, you will see how the print working directory command tells you the exact path you occupy, how the change directory command accepts both absolute paths from the root and relative paths from your current folder, and why pagers like less are preferable for huge logs. Practice sequences from creating nested directories to moving a file and viewing it are included so you can build muscle memory. By the end of this chapter you will have a small set of commands that let you explore, inspect, modify, and clean up a RHEL system with confidence and care.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to navigate the Linux filesystem confidently, perform basic file and directory operations, inspect file contents with pagers, and identify file types. Each objective focuses on a real administrative skill: locating where you are with the print working directory, changing context with change directory, and listing contents with useful options so you can diagnose permission and ownership issues quickly. You will also create and remove directories and files, learn recursive and parent-friendly creation, and practice safe deletion patterns to avoid irreversible mistakes. Viewing files with cat, less, and more helps you inspect configuration and log files without risking system state. Finally, you'll use file and long listing formats to identify whether an item is a text file, executable, or binary. Each objective contains short practice prompts and a milestone that ties the command to a validated competency. These objectives are intentionally practical so you can apply them on a real RHEL VM as soon as you finish.

Beyond command names, you need reliable patterns and safety checks. This screen outlines practice goals: using mkdir with -p to build nested directories in one step, copying a template tree recursively with cp -r, and moving files while preserving content and names with mv. We also stress deletion safety: rmdir only removes empty directories, rm -r removes recursively, and rm -f forces removal without prompts. A simple habit like using rm -i during practice prevents accidental data loss. Practice scenarios guide you through creating a projects tree, adding index files, moving and renaming files, then cleaning up safely. Each practice step builds both muscle memory and a mental checklist you can use on a live server. The milestone is a short command sequence you should be able to execute reliably on your RHEL VM without supervision.

The Linux filesystem is a single tree that starts at the root directory, known as forward slash. Everything on the system — configuration files, user data, binaries, devices — branches from that root. Understanding this single-root model helps you reason about absolute and relative paths. An absolute path starts at the root and lists every directory to the target, for example forward slash etc forward slash hosts. A relative path describes how to reach the target from where you currently are, using names and the special entries dot and dot dot to mean the current and parent directory. Practically, this matters because commands like change directory and file operations can accept either form. When you use absolute paths you remove ambiguity — you always operate on the same location regardless of where you are. Relative paths are faster to type and often more convenient during interactive work, but they depend on your current working directory. A common misconception is that home is the root; it is not. Home is just a directory under root, typically under slash home slash yourusername. Learning to read and compose both absolute and relative paths avoids mistakes when moving or deleting files and helps you write reliable scripts. Think about building a mental map: when you see a path, imagine the branch sequence from the root to the leaf and verify before you act.

Knowing your current directory and being able to change it reliably is a daily task. The print working directory command reports the absolute path to your shell's current location; use it to confirm context before running scripts or editing files. The change directory command accepts an absolute path or a relative one. For example, cd /etc moves to the system configuration folder, while cd projects moves to a child directory in your current folder. Special shortcuts speed up navigation: cd tilde returns you to your home directory regardless of where you are. cd double dot moves you up one level, useful for stepping out of nested folders quickly. cd hyphen toggles back to the previous directory you were in — that is handy during troubleshooting when you hop between two locations. When you chain these commands in a session, a reliable pattern is to run pwd, then cd to the target, then run pwd again to verify. A common error is assuming cd without arguments always does nothing; it actually moves you to your home directory. Another pitfall is forgetting how relative paths change meaning based on your current directory. Practice sequences such as creating a nested tree, moving into it, printing the working directory, and then returning using cd - will build this mental model. Ask yourself: before running a command that alters files, what path does pwd show and is that the intended location?

Listing directory contents is more than seeing filenames. The basic list command shows names, but combining options reveals crucial metadata. Use ls -l to get a long listing that includes file permissions, number of links, owner, group, size, and modification time. This output helps you identify whether a file is writable, executable, or owned by another user. Hidden files, those that begin with a dot, are not shown by default; ls -a reveals them. Often you want both metadata and hidden entries, so ls -la or ls -al is the common combination. A frequent misunderstanding is mixing up the columns in ls -l: the first column shows permission bits and file type, not just an attribute label. The long listing prefix begins with a character denoting file type, like dash for a regular file or d for a directory, followed by permission triplets. Reading this line quickly is a necessary skill for troubleshooting permissions and diagnosing why a service can't read its configuration. Practice reading ls -l output and spotting whether a file is owned by root or your user, whether it is executable, and when it was last modified. If you cannot find a configuration file, remember to run ls -a to show dotfiles and avoid the common mistake of assuming the file does not exist.

Creating directories and empty files is routine. The make directory command creates directories by name. When you need to create nested parents in one step, use the -p option: mkdir -p /tmp/new_app/config will build any missing directories in the chain. Removing directories uses rmdir, but rmdir only succeeds when the target is empty. That behavior prevents accidental removal of nested content. Another pitfall is assuming mkdir will prompt before overwriting — it will not overwrite existing directories and will return success if the directory already exists unless prevented. Practice with small test directories and use interactive deletion to build safe habits.

Copy and move are often confused because they both change where data appears. The copy command duplicates files or directories, leaving the original in place. For a single file, cp source. txt destination. txt creates a new file with the same contents. When the destination is a directory, cp places the file inside it. Copying directories requires the recursive option: cp -r directory1 directory2 will duplicate the full tree. The move command renames or relocates files; mv oldname. txt newname. txt is a rename, while mv myfile. txt /tmp moves the file into another directory without keeping a second copy.
